extracted.intended_audience: students and beginning researchers learning to write and evaluate academic arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assembling, evaluating, and defending claims in academic writing: how to select, report, and test evidence; anticipate and respond to objections; and state warrants that connect reasons to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer primary sources and show the chain of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Data taken from sources are shaped by those sources and by intervening reports; readers expect you to use primary sources or get as close to them as possible and to provide complete citations and a bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how many removes you are from original data; prefer primary sources when feasible; provide full citations so readers can trace the chain of reporting; be thoughtful about whose data you use and how you use them. Example: government reports vs. third-party media reports of celebrity incomes — be aware of how the data were compiled and acknowledge potential errors in intervening reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow field-specific standardized methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Each area of study has standardized procedures for collecting and reporting evidence; observing those procedures encourages readers to accept your evidence without seeing it themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using secondary sources, note what kind of evidence they cite and how they cite it, then do likewise. 'When in sociology, do as sociologists do.' If you depart from common methods, explain and justify the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate evidence for accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect evidence to be accurate; a trivial factual mistake can undermine trust in the entire argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record data completely and clearly; double-check facts before, during, and after writing. If evidence is dubious, acknowledge its dubious quality — pointing to unreliable evidence and rejecting it can demonstrate caution and trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be appropriately precise
rubrics_metrics.description: State evidence and claims with appropriate precision; vague hedges (some, many, often) can prevent readers from assessing your claim's substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete numbers or definitions when possible. Recognize that 'appropriate' precision is field-dependent (e.g., physicists measure tiny fractions of seconds; historians may use months or years). Avoid excessive false precision (e.g., claiming a historical event happened at an exact minute). Watch for hedging words that obscure assessability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient and representative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect enough evidence to support a claim and that evidence to represent the full range of variation in the available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on a single quotation, number, or anecdote for a broad claim. If using sampled data, demonstrate sample representativeness; when evidence is from a small sample, show why it is typical or admit limits. Seek more evidence where readers are likely to demand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers consider who provided the evidence; authority affects how much weight evidence carries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer expert or otherwise authoritative sources for claims where authority matters. If a source lacks authority, acknowledge that limitation and explain why you still consider the evidence relevant (or why you ignore it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider relevance (anticipate reader expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect evidence to be relevant to the claim; relevance is a central criterion though treated in more detail elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble evidence that directly bears on your claim; anticipate that readers will challenge whether a reason actually supports the claim and be prepared to justify relevance, often through warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report evidence accurately and completely
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful reporting of how you collected or obtained data fosters reader trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record observations and data fully, present them clearly (tables, charts, etc.), and double-check transcription and calculation errors. If you tidy or reframe data for presentation, be transparent about those decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test your argument as your readers will
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalizing, read your argument imagining a reader who wants you to be wrong; question the problem, the solution, and the support just as critics will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Why is there a problem? Why have you defined it this way? Does your solution match the problem? Have you overstated the claim? Why is your solution better than alternatives? Do your reasons and evidence support the claim? If you can't answer, find answers or revise the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and acknowledge plausible objections and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: No argument is complete without acknowledging and responding to other points of view; doing so increases credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine predictable questions and objections (intrinsic soundness, extrinsic alternatives). Acknowledge alternatives you can rebut, important lines in your field, conclusions readers prefer, evidence they know, and counterexamples you must explain. Don't overwhelm readers with too many acknowledgments — aim for 'just right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select which objections to respond to strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose objections to address based on their plausibility and importance rather than addressing all possible objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize: (1) plausible weaknesses you can rebut; (2) alternative lines important in the field; (3) alternative conclusions readers want; (4) alternative evidence readers know; (5) important counterexamples. Prefer objections that let you restate or reinforce parts of your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge questions you cannot answer candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you discover a serious flaw you cannot fix, candid acknowledgment is better than hiding it, as honesty preserves credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit the flaw and offer responses such as: the rest of the argument balances the flaw; more research could resolve it; the flaw limits full acceptance but the argument still offers insight. When possible, transform an unprovable claim into a testable hypothesis and show results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame responses as subordinate arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to alternatives should not be mere dismissals; they should be supported by reasons, evidence, and possibly warrants (i.e., subordinate arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minimal response may suffice if its basis is obvious; otherwise present reasons and evidence to justify rejecting or limiting the alternative. Use additional acknowledgments and responses as needed to thicken and strengthen your overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an appropriate vocabulary and tone for acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: How you introduce and phrase acknowledgments affects perceived respectfulness and persuasive force — there is a range from dismissive to respectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to acknowledge (from more dismissive to more respectful): use despite/regardless/notwithstanding or although/while/even though; signal tentativeness with seem/appear/may; attribute the view to unnamed or named sources; acknowledge in your own voice with concession words (admittedly, granted, to be sure). Avoid ad hominem tones; critize the work, not the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear strategies to introduce and attribute alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Different linguistic strategies give different weight to the alternative you acknowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect signal: 'seems'/'appears'; unnamed attribution: 'It is easy to think...'; specific attribution: 'Some have argued...'; concession phrasing: 'It is true that..., however...' Choose phrasing based on how much weight you want to assign the alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to objections with the right degree of bluntness and civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses can range from tactful questioning to blunt rejection; choose tone based on how flawed the alternative appears and always focus criticism on arguments, not persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open a response with but/however/on the other hand. Possible responses: express confusion ('I do not quite understand how...'); note unsettled issues; claim irrelevance or unreliability ('the evidence is shaky'); or bluntly label an argument weak or untenable while remaining civil. When suggesting mistakes, do so diplomatically and focus on the evidence or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate three predictable reader disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers commonly object via (1) pointing to additional causes, (2) offering counterexamples, or (3) disputing definitions; anticipate and address these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you focus on one cause, acknowledge others and explain your emphasis. For counterexamples, acknowledge plausible interesting exceptions and explain why they don't overturn your claim (e.g., statistical reasoning). When definitions matter, define terms to support your solution and argue for your chosen definition while acknowledging alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and test warrants that connect reasons to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A warrant is the general statement that links a specific reason to a claim (When X, then Y). Readers may challenge a reason by questioning its relevance, which requires either an explicit or implicit warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make warrants explicit when writing for non-experts or when readers could question relevance. Deconstruct compressed warrants into general circumstance → general consequence form and test whether the warrant reliably supports the inference. Use warrants to show why a reason bears on the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form warrants at the appropriate level of generality and test their reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants must be more general than the specific reason/claim and should be tested by asking whether the general circumstance legitimately implies the general consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose arguments to locate the warrant, then evaluate whether the general principle holds across relevant instances. Be prepared to defend warrants that specialists take for granted when writing for broader audiences (e.g., 'shared DNA measures species relationship').
